\subsection{Transfer-learning protocol}
\label{sec:sota-protocol}

Two pretrained lightweight architectures were adapted to EuroSAT:
MobileNetV2, built from the depthwise separable blocks of
Section~\ref{sec:task2}, and EfficientNet-B0. Both start from torchvision's
ImageNet weights. The final linear layer of each classifier is replaced by a
new ten-class prediction layer, and every run uses the same stratified split,
random seed, augmentation, training-split normalisation statistics, batch
size of 128, 30-epoch budget and Tesla~T4 as the custom models. The checkpoint
is again chosen by lowest validation loss, before the test split is touched.

The lecture notes give two options once the new prediction layer is in place:
keep the pretrained backbone \emph{frozen}, or \emph{fine-tune} it. Each
network was run both ways, so the choice is measured rather than assumed.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Frozen.} Only the new prediction layer is trained, with Adam at
  a learning rate of $10^{-3}$. The backbone acts as a fixed feature extractor,
  and its batch-normalisation statistics are held at their ImageNet values.
  \item \textbf{Fine-tuned.} Every weight is trained, starting from the same
  ImageNet weights, with Adam at a learning rate of $10^{-4}$. The smaller rate
  keeps the pretrained filters from being destroyed by the large, random
  gradients of the untrained head in the first epochs. This is the rate used
  in the Keras EfficientNet fine-tuning example that the brief cites.
\end{itemize}

The primary runs keep the input at $64\times64$, the resolution the custom
models see. That is the only like-for-like comparison with Model~B, and it is
what an edge device would actually be given. Because ImageNet networks are
designed for $224\times224$ input, a supplementary pair repeats each network
with the $64\times64$ images upsampled to $224\times224$. Each supplementary
pair differs from its primary pair in input size only, so the ablation
isolates what resolution buys.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:sota-results}

  \centering

  % box \generatedtable shows before the runs exist cannot sit in a \resizebox.
  \footnotesize
  \setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
  \generatedtable{tables/sota_comparison.tex}{\#22}
  \caption{Pretrained lightweight models on the EuroSAT test split. Precision
  and recall are macro averages over the ten classes. \emph{Trained} counts the
  parameters updated during training. Sizes are in MB, measured from the saved
  weights; the custom models in Table~\ref{tab:custom-comparison} are in KB.
  The supplementary rows upsample the $64\times64$ images to $224\times224$.}
  \label{tab:sota-comparison}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:sota-comparison} lists both strategies for each network. Two
columns are worth reading together. \emph{Parameters} and \emph{Size} are
identical for the frozen and fine-tuned runs of a network, because freezing
changes what is trained, not what is deployed. \emph{Trained} is where they
differ: a frozen backbone updates only the prediction layer, well under one
per cent of the network, against every weight when fine-tuned. Any accuracy
gap between the two rows of a pair is therefore bought with training effort
alone, at no cost in memory or in operations per image.

For both networks that gap is large. Fine-tuning raises every metric well
above the frozen feature extractor. The likely explanation is a domain shift.
ImageNet filters were learnt on close-range photographs of objects, while
EuroSAT is overhead satellite imagery at a much coarser scale. A frozen
backbone can only re-weight features that were learnt for the wrong kind of
image; fine-tuning lets the filters themselves move towards field boundaries,
road textures and water.

The two architectures also rank differently under the two strategies. Frozen,
EfficientNet-B0 is clearly the weaker network, despite having almost twice
MobileNetV2's parameters. Fine-tuned, the two are practically level. The
frozen gap therefore says how well each network's ImageNet features happen to
transfer to $64\times64$ overhead images, not how much each network can learn.
EfficientNet-B0's compound scaling assumes $224\times224$ input, and at
$64\times64$ its downsampling stages leave a $2\times2$ final feature map; its
fixed features suffer more from the small input than MobileNetV2's do. Once
fine-tuned, however, EfficientNet-B0 offers no meaningful accuracy over
MobileNetV2 for nearly twice the memory. MobileNetV2 is the better edge
candidate of the two.

The supplementary rows show that resolution and fine-tuning are partly
substitutes. Upsampling to $224\times224$ gives both frozen backbones a gain of
several points, but the fine-tuned models gain less than one. A frozen
network's filters are fixed at ImageNet's object scale, so enlarging the input
is the only way to bring the data to them. Fine-tuning instead moves the
filters to the data, after which resolution matters much less: for each
network, the fine-tuned $64\times64$ model outperforms the frozen
$224\times224$ one. It does so at about $(224/64)^2\approx12$ times fewer
operations per image, because a convolution's cost scales with the $H\times W$
of its output and the network is otherwise unchanged. For an edge device,
fine-tuning at native resolution is the cheaper way to get accuracy.

Even the smallest of these models is one to two orders of magnitude larger on
disk than Model~B (Table~\ref{tab:custom-comparison}). That is why the two tables
use different units. Whether the extra accuracy is worth that memory is the
question Section~\ref{sec:task6} answers.
